findings.finding: The note says both editors draw on Cluny's customs, and the new sentence says the link 'rests on these two early twentieth-century editors'. Both works are vendored. Hunter Blair's 1907 notes do cite the Ordo Cluniacensis. Gasquet's text never names Cluny. His only line that bears on the link is that the Rule was 'practically the only monastic Rule of the West' from the ninth to the twelfth century. So the Cluny claim rests on Hunter Blair alone, and the note implies both carry it. The brief says such a note must not imply both accounts carry a fact that rests on only one. This was already wrong in release 19; the rewrite repeats it and adds a sentence that makes it stronger.
findings.evidence: grep -i 'clu[gn]|cluni|ordo|customar|consuetud' cic/texts/benedict_rule-of-saint-benedict_gasquet1925.txt finds no match (4,949 lines). The Gasquet line is at lines 580-581: 'ninth to the twelfth century, when it was practically / the only monastic Rule of the West'. cic/texts/benedict_rule-of-st-benedict-lat-eng_hunter-blair1907.txt lines 10525-10527: 'the Ordo Cluniacensis , of the 11th century, lays down fixed rules and times for conversation in the cloister'; Cluny is also named at lines 10805, 10869, 10940, 11036, 11053 and 11061. The Gasquet header says 'Gasquet's introduction is scholarship of 1909', so 'early twentieth-century' is right for both editors.
findings.required_fix: note = "Oswald Hunter Blair was a Benedictine editor of the Rule. In 1907 he drew on the later customs of Cluny to show how it was lived. Cardinal Gasquet, another Benedictine editor, calls the Rule practically the only rule for monks in the West from the ninth to the twelfth century. He does not name Cluny. This rests on these two editors, not on Cluny's own texts. It has not yet been checked against a modern study." (score_turn: FRE 66.7, FK 7.1; longest sentence 24 words, which is the existing Gasquet sentence). Optional, since ruling 3 allows it: both works are vendored, so the two sources could carry file, lines and quote, for example Hunter Blair lines 10525-10527 'the Ordo Cluniacensis , of the 11th century, lays down fixed rules and times for conversation in the cloister' and Gasquet lines 580-581 'when it was practically the only monastic Rule of the West'. Validator-checked quotes would then make the link verified-direct / A.

findings.finding: The new note says the link 'rests on two older works: an 1871 edition of Alfred's English text, and James Barmby'. Sweet's edition is not vendored and no one in the project has read it. It reaches the link only through Barmby's footnote. Barmby's 1895 introduction is vendored (NPNF 2nd series vol. 12), and it carries both facts in the note. So the note presents a work known only from a citation as a second support. The older wording, 'We have this from James Barmby', was accurate.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/npnf212_leo-great-gregory-great.xml lines 24031-24038: 'This is asserted by Alfred the Great, who, nearly three hundred years afterwards, with the assistance of his divines, made a translation, or rather paraphrase, of it in the West Saxon tongue, intending, as he says, to send a copy to every bishop in his Kingdom' with note 1261: 'Edited, with an English version, by Henry Sweet of Balliol College, and published for the Early English Text Society, 1871, Part I., p. 7.' No Sweet or EETS file is in cic/texts/.
findings.required_fix: note = "King Alfred had Gregory's Pastoral Rule put into West Saxon English. He said he meant to send a copy to each bishop in his kingdom. We have this from James Barmby, Gregory's translator, writing in 1895. He points to an 1871 edition of Alfred's English text. It has not yet been checked against a modern study." (FRE 69.0, FK 6.3). Optional, under ruling 3: the Barmby source could carry file cic/texts/npnf212_leo-great-gregory-great.xml, lines 24033-24035 and quote 'made a translation, or rather paraphrase, of it in the West Saxon tongue, intending, as he says, to send a copy to every bishop in his Kingdom'. The validator would check it, and the link would then be verified-direct / A.

findings.finding: The note says 'This rests on two older accounts, from 1842 and 1921.' Every fact in the note comes from Conybeare (1921). The 1842 source is Blackmore's note on the dissenters' monasteries in 1830. It says only that three or four have returned to the Church, and it carries none of the note's facts: not 1799, not Plato, not the sixteen terms, not Paul I, not the old books, not the name Edinoverie. The drafter's doubt is correct.
findings.evidence: conybeare_russian-dissenters_1921.txt lines 5522-5540 carry the 1799 request for priests and chrism, the sixteen conditions examined by Plato and sanctioned by Paul I on 27 October 1800, and 'permission to use the old books'. Line 5861 has 'Iedinovierie, as it is called'. mouravieff_history-of-the-church-of-russia_blackmore1842.txt lines 19636-19641 are about the twenty-six dissenters' monasteries: 'Only three or four have in the course of the last century returned into the bosom of the Church.'
findings.required_fix: note = "In 1799 Old Believers in Moscow asked the official church for priests and holy oil. Metropolitan Plato looked over their sixteen terms, and in 1800 Tsar Paul I approved them. The terms let them keep the old books under priests of the church. The arrangement came to be called Edinoverie. This rests on one older account, by F. C. Conybeare in 1921. It has not yet been checked against a modern study." (FRE 73.0, FK 5.2)

findings.finding: One link of the class was missed, in era 4. It is graded Dominant Modern Reconstruction, and its only support is one pre-1930 secondary account: F. Ll. Griffith (1913), quoted twice. That is exactly ruling 1 of 'Whole-set rulings', which P2-L11b should have applied. It is not in P2-L11b's ruling1 or ruling1_other_links lists, and P2-L11c did not catch it either. The only modern study on the Makurian movement is Welsby (2002). The census cites it as 'the standard accessible synthesis' and, at ch. 3, 'On Kyriakos and Makurian–Egyptian relations'. It is not cited for the Coptic alphabet or for Coptic monks and books. P2-L11b's own test did not count a general survey of that kind (it ruled the same way on Franklin and Shepard, 'the standard English history'). So no repo-cited modern study supports this reading. This applies a ruling already made, not a new decision.

findings.finding: 'No modern study is at hand' can read as 'no modern study exists'. For three of the six, the repo itself names a modern study of the very subject. Andrews, The Early Humiliati (1999), covers the Humiliati, though it is cited for their decline. Rosenwein, Rhinoceros Bound (1982), covers Cluny. Franklin and Shepard (1996) and Vlasto (1970) cover the Rus' and Slavic movements. None of these is cited for these readings, and none has been read. What is true is that none has been checked for this reading. That is the drafter's Humiliati doubt, and it applies to all six. Change the wording in every note, so the six read alike.
